title: Que tempo faz? — weather, months and dates
goal: Talk about the weather with three different verbs, name the months and seasons, then write the date the way people in Portugal write it.

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Um novembro chuvoso
dialogs.intro: It's been raining since dawn. Budi comes down to the kitchen with wet hair, and Dona Fernanda laughs.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Então? Que tempo faz lá fora?
lines.id: Well? What's the weather like out there?
lines.literal: so? what weather makes there outside?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Está a chover. E está muito vento.

lines.literal: is to rain. and is much wind.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Em novembro é sempre assim. Em dezembro chove ainda mais.
lines.id: November's always like this. In December it rains even more.
lines.literal: in November is always so. in December rains still more.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Na Indonésia também chove muito, mas nunca faz frio.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não temos inverno. Temos duas estações: chuva e sol.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Que sorte! Aqui o inverno é curto, mas é húmido.
lines.id: Lucky you! Here winter is short, but it's damp.
lines.literal: what luck! here the winter is short, but is humid.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E o verão? Faz muito calor?

lines.text: Em julho e agosto faz muito calor, sobretudo no Alentejo. Quarenta graus.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: A primavera é a melhor altura. Abril, maio: está fresco e há flores.

notes: **Month names are written in lowercase.** *janeiro*, *fevereiro*, *março* — unlike English. Days of the week are lowercase too: *segunda-feira*, *domingo*. Only names of people, cities and countries are capitalized.
**Sobretudo** means "especially" or "above all" — a very common word in both written and spoken Portuguese. Similar words: *principalmente*, *especialmente*.

**A altura** in the sense of "time" or "period" is typically European Portuguese: *nessa altura* (at that time), *na altura do Natal* (around Christmas). In Brazil people say *época*. The same word also means "height".
**Nem no inverno?** — *nem* means "not even", and it strengthens the earlier negation. *Nem eu* = "neither do I", the standard reply to a negative statement.

**Está muito vento**, not *faz vento*. Wind and rain use *estar* in Portugal; temperature uses *fazer*. The rule is laid out in the table below — and to be honest, Portuguese speakers sometimes mix them up themselves.
**Húmido with an h.** European spelling writes *húmido*, while Brazil writes *úmido*. This small difference shows up in a few other words too, like *facto* (Portugal) versus *fato* (Brazil).

grammars.title: Three verbs for the weather
body: All of them are used without a real subject, much like English "it" in "it's raining", where nobody is doing the raining.

head: Verb
Used for
Example
rows: *Faz frio. Faz calor. Faz bom tempo.*

after: **Chover and nevar have only one form**, the third person: *chove*, *choveu*, *está a chover*. Nobody says "I rain" in any language.

To ask: *Que tempo faz?* ("what's the weather like?") or *Como está o tempo?*. Note that *o tempo* means "weather" **and** "time" — context tells them apart: *não tenho tempo* (I don't have time), *está bom tempo* (the weather's nice).

grammars.title: Months and seasons
body: Months take the preposition *em*; seasons take *em* contracted with the article.
after: The four seasons: **a primavera** (spring), **o verão** (summer), **o outono** (autumn, fall), **o inverno** (winter). The preposition contracts: *na primavera*, *no verão*, *no outono*, *no inverno*.
With months there's no contraction: *em janeiro*, *em agosto* — simple. Same for years: *em 2026* (read *dois mil e vinte e seis*).

grammars.title: Writing and saying the date
body: The order is day of the week, date, month, year — as in British English — all linked with *de*.
after: **Dates use ordinary numbers, not ordinals.** *5 de maio* is read *cinco de maio*, not *quinto*. That's different from English "the fifth", and easier.
*Fazer anos* means to have a birthday — literally "to make years". *Quando fazes anos?* = "when's your birthday?", answered *Faço anos a vinte de março.*

blocks.text: Temperature is given in *graus*: *Estão vinte graus* (it's twenty degrees) or *Faz vinte graus*. Below zero: *menos dois graus*. And the weather forecast is *a previsão do tempo* — a phrase you'll hear every evening on Portuguese TV. Temperatures are always in Celsius.

blocks.title: A year in Portugal, through Budi's tropical eyes
items: **The biggest difference isn't temperature but day length.** In late December the sun sets at five in the afternoon; in late June, at nine in the evening. In Indonesia the sun sets around six all year round. This is what surprises newcomers from the equator most.
Portuguese winters rarely freeze — Lisbon seldom drops below five degrees — but old houses often have no heating, so it can feel colder inside than out. Bring layers, not one thick coat.

*Agosto* is the national holiday month: many shops and small restaurants close, especially in Lisbon, as their owners head back to their hometowns. If you visit then, don't be surprised to find your favorite tasca locked up for the whole month.
